key_gap: Both solved the straw-bridge puzzle with the same physics (Euler ~45 g, deck fails ~40-80 g, triangulated truss with bundled chords, ~2x margin), but the human won on the style's home ground: it used the constraint list as a generative operator, converting each constraint into a principle ('the only thing that pulls is the rubber band'), then ran an iterative tightening pass — imposing stricter self-constraints (both bands must earn their place as pre-tensioned lashings, tape budget caps, exact symmetry) to force refinement — and landed the design in one pass. The AI treated the constraints as a boundary to satisfy: it enumerated and complied with them (sound truss, correct budget), then spent its extra passes on verification and the decision packet instead of further constrained refinement, and so produced a compliant-but-less-refined design at higher token cost.
learning_signal: Constraint lists are not fences — they are generative operators. The elite move is iterative constraint-augmentation: after a workable design, deliberately tighten the constraint set (fewer resources, extra symmetry, higher margin, force every kit element to earn its place) and re-run ideation; each tightening produces a simpler or more robust design. Comply-and-stop (treating constraints only as limits to satisfy) yields sound but unrefined solutions, and spending the saved budget on meta-narrative does not recover the lost refinement.
suggested_improvement: In HOW, after selecting a workable candidate, add a mandatory 'constraint-tightening pass': impose 2-3 stricter self-constraints on the selected design (e.g., every allowed material must appear in a load-bearing role, cap the tape/material budget, require symmetry) and re-generate at least one refinement alternative; promote the refinement if it ties or dominates on compliance with better margin or simplicity. Record the tightening chain in the decision packet as 'constraint ancestry' so the refinement is auditable.

key_gap: The pure style treated the 'zero third-party dependencies' rule as gospel: it produced a beautiful 5,000-LOC stdlib-only stack, even compressed the schedule to 3.5 months to fit the deadline, and explicitly refused to question the rule ('A constraint is a constraint') — the tell of constraint-worship. The AI ran a constraint audit before constraining the search space: classified the rule as artificial/waivable (owned by the security team, with a documented routine waiver path), computed cost of compliance (~6 person-months, hand-rolled auth risk) vs cost of removal (2 days + one waiver email), and selected the waiver + pinned audited library, replacing the blunt rule with a precise one (one pinned, audited, vendored dependency) that preserves the supply-chain intent.
learning_signal: Before constraining the search space, audit the constraint: separate genuine constraints (deadline, team size, physics) from artificial ones (self-imposed rules, owned policies, waivable defaults). An artificial constraint that costs more to serve than to remove is the real bottleneck — serving it is constraint-worship, and 'creative within the rule' is how the style produces elaborate wrongness. The correct move is to escalate/waive and replace the blunt rule with a precise one that preserves the original intent (e.g., pin + audit instead of zero dependencies).
suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory 'constraint audit' gate in WHAT before treating any stated constraint as hard: for each constraint record (a) origin and owner, (b) genuine vs artificial classification (is it waivable/escalatable?), (c) cost of compliance vs cost of removal, (d) the waiver path and who holds it. If any constraint is artificial and removal dominates, route the task toward ESCALATED or add the waiver request as a deliverable; never enter HOW with an unaudited artificial constraint serving as a design fence.
